Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself with a smaller piece of that same problem. For it to work, there must be a "base case" — a simple condition where the function just returns a known answer instead of calling itself again, which prevents infinite looping. A classic example is calculating factorial: factorial(5) is 5 × factorial(4), and factorial(4) is 4 × factorial(3), all the way down until you reach factorial(1), which simply returns 1. Once you grasp it, recursion becomes a powerful way to tackle problems like traversing trees, sorting lists, or exploring mazes, because it naturally mirrors how those problems break down into smaller sub-problems.
